Portfolio

A portfolio is a group or securities or other investments. If you invest in a diversified portfolio of securities, you can generally reduce your investment risk. (Investment risk is the volatility of investment returns of the securities in your portfolio.) A diversified portfolio lets you to earn a higher rate of return for a given amount of risk or reduce your risk for a given rate of return.
Annuities are big business. According to the Insurance Information Institute, annuity sales totaled $310.6 billion in 2022, a 22.0% increase from 2021.

What are annuities and where do they fit in your portfolio? An annuity is a series of payments that you receive at regular intervals for a specific period. Most retirement annuities offer a monthly payment that you, the annuitant, receive until you die. The most popular types of retirement annuities are variable annuities. Variable annuities are tax-deferred investments that millions of Americans buy to supplement their retirement incomes.
The following table summarizes the basic types of annuities:
Annuity due

An annuity due is an annuity that is paid/received at the beginning of each period. An ordinary annuity is paid or received at the end of each period. Because you receive an annuity due sooner than an ordinary annuity, its payout period ends sooner.
An annuity due is a payment that you receive at the beginning of each period. An ordinary annuity is a payment that you receive at the end of each period.

There are fixed and variable annuities. Fixed annuities pay a fixed amount that is based on a fixed interest rate. Equity-indexed annuities are fixed annuities that pay more if the stock index to which the annuity is pegged performs better than expected. Equity-indexed annuities require an extra fee. Variable annuities pay an amount that varies with the investment performance of mutual fund-like investments called subaccounts that are sold with a variable-annuity contract.

There are also immediate and deferred annuities. As you can guess, immediate annuities start to make payments immediately; they don't accumulate. Deferred annuities start payments later. The money you invest grows during a deferred annuity's accumulation period. The annuity commencement date signifies the beginning of a deferred annuity's payout period.

An annuity is a contract that you buy from a life-insurance company when you make an initial purchase payment. In exchange for the payment, you receive an immediate or deferred annuity. The contract explains the terms of annuitization. It also explains the payment amount (if a fixed annuity), value of purchase payments, accumulation period, payout period, and other contract options you've paid for.

As contract owner, you should be as familiar as possible with the terms of your annuity. It isn't necessary for you to be the annuitant. You can just as easily buy an annuity contract for someone else.

Some annuity contracts are bought with a single purchase payment. For example, you may decide to make a single purchase payment of $250,000, invested at a guaranteed fixed rate of 8%. In exchange, you receive an immediate monthly annuity of $2,900 for the next 20 years. If you later decided to add to your initial purchase payment in order to extend or increase your annuity, you can make additional purchase payments. In general, you aren't allowed to make additional payments once you begin to receive payments.

Variable annuities combine features of mutual funds and life insurance. This results in variable annuities often being called hybrid financial products. Financial planners and brokers are fond of describing variable annuities as "a mutual fund in a life-insurance wrapper."

When you buy a variable annuity, you invest your purchase payments in a range of mutual fund-like investments called subaccounts. A variable annuity may have several subaccounts from which to choose, each with its own investment objective. Like mutual funds, the investment performance of subaccounts varies from year to year. The volatility of returns from year to year is why these annuities are called variable annuities. It's very important that you read the subaccount prospectus before making investment decisions.

A variable annuity's unit price is called its accumulated unit value. AUV is similar to a mutual fund's net asset value. Subaccounts are essentially the same investment as the underlying mutual fund. The same portfolio manager and team of investment professionals are responsible for investment decisions, and both are subject to the same investment restrictions.

As a financial product sold by life insurance companies, it's no surprise that annuities have a life insurance feature. Annuities pay a death benefit to the beneficiary if the annuitant dies before payments begin. The death benefit is usually the larger of the contract value or net amount of purchase payments.

Annuity contract owners can also buy options that resemble those available for life insurance policies. These options include a guaranteed minimum payout, enhanced death benefit, and joint-and-survivor option.
Annuities for retirement

Life-insurance companies often sell investors variable annuities to provide income in retirement. Annuities supplement other sources of retirement income, including pensions, IRAs, and Social Security.

Annuities insure against such events as the untimely death of the annuitant. In the event an annuitant dies before receiving the contract value of the annuity, a death benefit is paid to the beneficiary.

A death benefit is also paid if the annuitant dies before the annuity commencement date or before a certain point in the payout period. You can also buy a joint-and-survivor option, which guarantees continued payments to your spouse if there is no death benefit.

Variable annuities are tax-deferred investments. Growth in the value of an annuity is not taxed until the money is paid to the beneficiary. However, the amount of purchase payments is generally not tax-deductible. These payments grow on a compounded basis, even after you begin to receive payments. Annuity payments are taxed as ordinary income to the extent that the payment represents growth in the value of the annuity. If things go as planned, you are in a lower tax bracket when you begin to receive payments.

You can begin to receive annuity payments, penalty-free, when you reach age 59-1/2. Because annuities are tax-advantaged accounts, you pay an early-withdrawal penalty equal to 10% of the withdrawal amount if you receive payments before you reach age 59-1/2.

Variable annuities add flexibility to your estate planning. You aren't required to receive annuity payments at age 72, the way you are with traditional IRAs and 401(k)s. In most cases, you aren't required to receive payments until you reach age 90. This flexibility allows you to leave more to your beneficiaries.

Unlike IRAs and 401(k)s, variable annuities have no dollar restrictions on purchases. However, it's important to evaluate advice from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to avoid buying variable annuities for IRAs or other tax-advantaged accounts.

Instead, you should aim to make maximum allowable contributions to 401(k)s and IRAs before buying variable annuities. 401(k)s and IRAs have substantially lower transaction costs than variable annuities. Variable annuities come with surrender charges as high as 9%, which drag down the investment performance of the annuity. Additionally, variable annuities have higher annual expenses than most IRAs and 401(k) plans.
Buying variable annuities
There are no dollar limits for buying variable annuities and there is seldom a transaction fee when you buy a variable annuity.

In comparison, IRAs allow you to contribute only up to $7,000 for 2024 ($8,000 if age 50 or older). The most an employee can contribute to a 401(k) plan for 2024 is the lesser of 100% of salary or $23,000 ($30,500 if 50 or older).

However, you face significant fees called surrender charges when you sell a variable annuity, particularly in the first few years. High surrender charges drag down an annuity contract's investment performance.

Surrender charges are often as high as 9% of withdrawals. Surrender charges are usually at their highest levels in the first year or two of owning the contract. Generally, surrender charges are levied on a sliding scale, declining 1 percentage point every year or two. This contract's surrender charge is 7% if withdrawn within one year of the initial purchase payment. Generally, most variable-annuity contracts allow you take out a minimum amount each year at no charge. A typical annuity allows free withdrawals each year of up to 10% of the contract value.

Before you buy a variable annuity, you should review it under the terms of its "free look" period, which is usually 10 days. The "free look" period allows a prospective contract owner to review the annuity at no charge or obligation.
According to the American Council of Life Insurers (ACLI), there are four main types of payout options:
Straight-life annuity. A straight-life annuity pays a fixed amount for the rest of your life. However, payments cease when you die. There are no payments to your beneficiary.

Joint-and-survivor annuity. A joint-and-survivor annuity is an expanded version of a straight-life annuity. After you die, it continues to make payments to your spouse or other beneficiary until they die. You are required to purchase an option for this extra coverage. Payments to your beneficiary can consist of either a lump sum or systematic withdrawals. You should consult a tax adviser to understand the tax treatment of lump-sum payments and systematic withdrawals.
Life income-with-refund annuity. A life income-with-refund annuity pays an annuity until you die. At your death, the life-insurance company returns to your beneficiary any unused purchase payments.

Life annuity with period-certain annuity. A life income-with-period-certain annuity pays an annuity until you die. If you die before a certain point in the payout period, the annuity continues to be paid to your beneficiary until that point in the payout period is reached.
Variable annuities & fees

Variable annuities are not cheap. In fact, their high fees are a big reason the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) suggests you consider variable annuities only as long-term investments. You should read the prospectus of an annuity you are considering buying to understand all fees. There are four main categories of fees:

Surrender charges. Surrender charges are also called deferred sales charges. These charges are paid if you withdraw money from a variable annuity before the end of the surrender period. Surrender charges are often as high as 9% of the amount withdrawn in the first and second years of a surrender period. The charge often declines by 1 percentage point each year for the rest of the period. The contract generally allows you to withdraw an amount each year that is free of a surrender charge. Hefty surrender charges hurt investment returns of your subaccounts more than other fees.

You may decide to exchange one annuity for another in a 1035 exchange. The transaction may qualify as a tax-free event, but you may owe surrender charges on the contract you are selling if you are still in the surrender charge period. In most cases, you will also have to begin a new surrender period for the contract you buy. To be sure of the tax consequences of a 1035 exchange, you should consult a tax adviser.

Mortality and expense fees. Mortality and expense fees are also called risk charges. You pay yearly M & E fees to the insurer to adjust for changes in the risk characteristics of its pool of insureds. M & E fees routinely add up to 1.25% of an annuity's contract value. On a $100,000 contract, 1.25% is equal to $1,250 a year.

Administrative fees. Administrative fees are also called contract maintenance fees. These fees are often charged at an annual flat rate of $25 to $30 per contract. If stated as a percentage, they are typically about 0.15% of contract value. On a $100,000 contract, 0.15% is equal to $150.

Management fees. Management fees are paid to the investment adviser, which is responsible for making investment decisions affecting your subaccounts. These fees are similar to the management fees paid to mutual funds. They are often about 0.75% to 1% of contract value. On a $100,000 contract, 0.75% is equal to $750.
The following table summarizes the impact of various fees on a $100,000 annuity. Except for surrender charges, these are fees paid every year:

In this case, yearly expenses are 2.15% to 2.40% of the annuity's contract value. In fact, average yearly fees for variable annuities generally lie in this range. These fees are 50 to 75 basis points higher than the average yearly fees for mutual funds.
Life insurers and their sales agents sometimes offer a bonus credit when you buy a variable annuity. For example, the insurer may add 3% to your contract value when you make a purchase payment.

The SEC urges that you evaluate bonus credit offers carefully. Bonus credits often have special terms and conditions, or include higher fees that show up later. These fees may include a higher surrender charge, higher M & E fees, or an extended surrender period.
Variable annuities & taxes
Variable annuities are investments for providing additional retirement income or meeting other long-term financial goals. Some of their tax advantages include:

Unlimited contributions. There are no yearly limits to how much you can contribute toward variable annuities. In comparison, IRAs and such employer-sponsored retirement plans as 401(k)s have yearly contribution limits. However, the Securities and Exchange Commission suggests that you contribute as much as you are allowed each year to IRAs and 401(k)s before buying annuities, particularly if your retirement plan at work receives matching contributions.

You can buy either qualified or nonqualified annuities. Qualified annuities are those annuities you buy for another tax-advantaged account. Since those accounts offer no additional tax advantages, the SEC advises you to buy nonqualified in most cases.

Tax-deferred growth. Most variable annuities are tax-deferred investments that accumulate on a compounded basis. Since you don't pay taxes until you receive annuity distributions, your investment grows to a larger sum.

The following table shows the benefits of compounding over time. The table assumes you invest $100,000 at 8%, compounded annually. The second column shows how much your tax-deferred contributions grow to at the end of each five-year period. The last three columns assume you pay income taxes at combined (federal and state) tax rates. For example, $100,000 invested for 20 years on a tax-deferred basis grows to $466,096, almost 57% more than if you had a combined tax rate of 30%. In this case, $100,000 would grow to only $297,357.

Flexibility in payout options. Variable annuities don't require that you begin your payout period at age 72. Traditional IRAs and 401(k) plans require you to begin taking required minimum distributions at this age, however. In many cases, variable annuities don't require a payout until you turn age 90.

This payout-deferral option adds flexibility to your estate planning. While passing on annuities to a beneficiary may not qualify as a tax-free event, you have the option to leave more than you could leave with a retirement account that requires minimum distributions every year.

While annuities generally allow you to withdraw a certain amount each year with no surrender charge, remember that you do pay an early-withdrawal penalty if you take a withdrawal before reaching age 59-1/2. You will also likely pay income taxes on some or all of the withdrawal.

Tax-free exchanges in most cases. Using a 1035 exchange allows you to buy and sell variable annuities without incurring capital gains. There are some exceptions to the rule, however. To make sure, you should consult a tax adviser if considering 1035 exchanges.
Mutual fund features
Buying a variable annuity is similar to buying a mutual fund for a tax-deferred account.

When you buy a mutual fund, you make an initial minimum investment. If it's an open-end fund, you buy shares at the fund's net asset value and pay a front-end load, if applicable. You can make additional investments for as little as $25. Additional investments allow you to dollar-cost average, a fundamental principle of investing. Moreover, since you're using a tax-deferred account by buying a variable annuity, your investment compounds over time.

When you buy a variable annuity, you make an initial purchase payment. Subsequent investments are called additional purchase payments. Your additional payments increase your annuity's contract value. Variable annuities seldom charge the equivalent of a front-end load.

Generally, you can make additional purchase payments during an annuity's accumulation period. Once the payout period begins, however, you're generally restricted from making additional purchase payments

When you buy a variable annuity, you invest your purchase payments in a range of mutual fund-like investments called subaccounts. A variable annuity may have several subaccounts from which to choose, each with its own investment objective. Like mutual funds, the investment performance of subaccounts varies from year to year, which is why these investments are called variable annuities. You should read the subaccount's prospectus before making investment decisions.

Subaccounts are essentially the same investment as the underlying mutual fund. The same portfolio manager and team of investment professionals are responsible for investment decisions, and both are subject to the same investment restrictions.

Variable annuities also report investment performance for their subaccounts the same way mutual funds do. This means they report average annual returns for periods of up to 10 years where available. A variable annuity's accumulated unit value shows the value of your contract on a unit basis, similar to a mutual fund's NAV. AUV also deducts some insurance-related expenses.

Similar to mutual funds, variable annuities have yearly operating expenses. The average expense ratio for mutual funds is about 0.25% to 1.0% per year. Variable annuities have an average expense ratio of about 2.25% per year. The difference in fees is largely explained by the higher mortality and expense fees, which average about 1.25% for annuity contracts.

When it comes to transaction fees, however, mutual funds are seldom as onerous as variable annuities. For example, there are thousands of no-load funds from which to choose. However, variable annuities charge a hefty surrender charge if you sell an annuity within a certain period after the initial purchase period. The surrender period routinely lasts six to seven years on variable annuities. Surrender charges are equivalent to a back-end load that you pay on a mutual fund.

Life insurance features
In addition to having features of a mutual fund, variable annuities have features of life insurance. After all, life-insurance companies sell variable annuities. Here are some similarities:

Designating a beneficiary. Life insurance policies and variable annuities require you to designate a beneficiary. In the event you die during an annuity's accumulation period, or before a certain point in the payout period, your beneficiary receives a death benefit. Your beneficiary is generally entitled to receive the greater amount of the annuity's contract value or value of purchase payments. Death benefits are paid as a lump sum or in systematic withdrawals. For an extra charge, you can usually buy an enhanced death benefit.

Payments based on investment performance. When you buy a life insurance policy, you pay a premium. With permanent life insurance, your premiums accumulate a cash value. Depending on the type of permanent life insurance coverage, some, or all, of your premiums are invested in bonds and other fixed income securities. Universal and variable universal life insurance policies let you switch to flexible premiums or stop paying premiums temporarily when your cash value grows to an adequate level.

With variable annuities, you invest your initial and any additional purchase payments in mutual fund-like investments called subaccounts. Your annuity contract likely consists of several subaccounts that span more than one investment objective. In years when your subaccounts have strong investment performance, you can usually make smaller payments, or even stop payments temporarily, to reflect the buildup in contract value.

Cash value accumulates to provide continued coverage. With permanent life insurance, the cash value of your policy continues to provide insurance coverage even if you stop making premium payments. (If you're buying term life insurance, your premiums do not accumulate a cash value and your policy lapses when you stop paying premiums.) In other words, the cash value is a reserve, or source, of future premiums that gives you flexibility.

It's helpful to think of a variable annuity's contract value in a similar way. The contract value is the source of annuity payments when the payout period begins. Strong investment performance boosts the contract value and gives you a respite from having to make additional purchase payments.

Optional premiums buy extra or enhanced coverage. With life insurance policies, you can often pay a premium to guarantee a minimum death benefit. Variable-annuity contracts also include options (at an extra charge) for guaranteeing a minimum annuity payment or death benefit. Guarantees are insurance in their purest form: a chance for you to swap uncertainty for certainty with an insurer that is willing to underwrite that risk in exchange for a fee.

Some variable-annuity contracts offer an option to buy long-term care insurance. Long-term care insurance is increasingly popular as the number of Americans who are age 60 or older rises dramatically over the next 20 years. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) advises you to evaluate carefully any annuities that sell long-term care insurance. It may be cheaper to buy a policy directly from a long-term care insurance provider.

Players in the industry

Four major categories of participants in the variable-annuities industry are life-insurance companies, credit rating agencies, annuity performance-evaluation services, and regulatory and industry groups. You, the prospective investor, are the fifth category.

Life-insurance companies. Some of the world's largest insurance companies sell variable annuities. This list includes such firms as Allianz Life, American Insurance Group, Equitable, Hartford Life, John Hancock, Mass Mutual, MetLife, Northwestern Mutual Life, and Prudential Life. Clearly, annuities are a reputable product with reputable firms backing them.

These insurance firms rely on a combination of their own agents, independent agents, and broker/dealers to sell annuities. Sales commissions on variable annuities are relatively high, which explains, in part, the high surrender charges on variable annuities.

Credit rating agencies. When you buy a variable annuity, it's important to have an idea of the insurer's credit rating. A credit rating is a credit rating agency's independent assessment of the insurer's ability to pay its claims on time and meet all other financial obligations. Usually, the top-notch ratings are triple-- or double--A. Ratings in the low--B range or lower signify deteriorating financial strength. The major credit ratings agencies include:

A.M. Best Co. A.M. Best Co. publishes financial-strength ratings called "Best's ratings" and financial performance rating for smaller companies. The New Jersey-based rating service reserves its top ratings for insurance companies with a very strong ability to meet their financial obligations. Firms with a single--C++ or lower rating are considered to have marginal, weak, or poor financial characteristics.

Standard & Poor's. Standard & Poor's has two sets of insurer ratings: a financial-strength rating and "financial-enhancement rating." It reserves its top-notch triple--A rating for firms with extremely strong financial characteristics. Firms with a double--B or lower rating are considered to have marginal or weak financial characteristics.

Fitch Ratings publishes two sets of insurer ratings: a Long-Term International Insurer Financial Strength, and Short-Term Insurer Financial Strength ratings. Fitch also reserves its top-notch triple--A rating for firms with exceptionally strong financial characteristics. Firms with a double--B or lower rating are considered to have moderately weak or weak financial characteristics.

Moody's Investors Service. Moody's also publishes financial-strength ratings of life insurance companies. Its top-tiered rating is also triple--A, which it assigns to insurers with exceptionally financial security. It describes as questionable those insurers to which it assigns a rating of "Ba" or lower.

TheStreet.com Ratings. TheStreet.com, which acquired Weiss Ratings in 2009, also publishes financial strength ratings of life insurers. Its Web site shows that its top rating is single-A and that single-D and below is weak.

Generally, you should aim to buy variable annuities from only those insurers that receive top-notch ratings over many years. After all, your annuity contract may not begin to annuitize for another 20 or 30 years. It also helps to check more than one source for a credit rating.

Annuity performance-evaluation services. Variable annuities invest in mutual fund-like subaccounts. This allows variable annuities to be evaluated by their investment performance in a similar fashion to evaluating mutual funds.

Some of these sources of variable annuities data include the Lipper Leaders rating system, Morningstar's Variable Annuity Performance Report, and Morningstar's MARC (Morningstar Annuity Research Center) Report.

Regulatory and industry-group participants. You may wish to see if the life insurer selling you a variable annuity is licensed in your state. For further information, visit the Web site of the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), which maintains a directory of state insurance departments.

If you believe the broker or agent misrepresented the terms and conditions of a variable-annuity contract, you can contact the Investor Complaint Center of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).
